extracted.intended_audience: in-house counsel, patent litigators, IP managers and advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating and avoiding willful patent infringement and enhanced damages after the Supreme Court's Halo decision, focused on how lower courts apply the Read factors and what defendants should do pre-suit to avoid enhancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #1: Whether the infringer deliberately copied the patentee's ideas or design
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the infringer deliberately copied the patentee's ideas or design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying is a powerful indicator of willfulness when paired with knowledge and no reasonable investigation. The article cites cases where long-term copying weighed heavily (e.g., Dominion v. Alstom) and where blatant copying was found (Sociedad Espanola), though pre-suit investigation can sometimes offset this factor if done in good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #2: Whether the infringer, upon knowing of the patent, investigated the scope of the patent and formed a good faith belief that it was invalid or that it was not infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the infringer, upon knowing of the patent, investigated the scope of the patent and formed a good faith belief that it was invalid or that it was not infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor is highlighted as one of the most salient post-Halo. Courts expect a reasonable, timely (pre-suit or during the infringement period) investigation and a bona fide belief formed then. Examples where such investigation avoided enhancement: Greatbatch v. AVX (opinions of counsel and design-arounds), Koninklijke Philips v. Zoll Medical. Examples where failure to investigate led to enhancement: Imperium v. Samsung, SRI v. Cisco.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #3: The infringer's litigation behavior
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Read list includes litigation conduct as a factor. While the article does not deeply unpack this factor, it is part of courts' nine-factor balancing when deciding enhanced damages under Halo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #4: The infringer's size and financial condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The infringer's size and financial condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider the defendant's size and financial condition (ability to pay) as one factor in awarding enhanced damages. The article lists this as part of the Read factors without extensive elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #5: The closeness of the case
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the infringement case was close (e.g., debatable claim construction, difficult technical issues) can mitigate against finding egregious conduct. The article notes 'closeness' is a Read factor relevant to the balancing analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #6: The duration of the infringer's misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of the infringer's misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longstanding misconduct or copying over an extended period weighs in favor of enhancement. The article cites Dominion where copying over a long period contributed to a finding for enhanced damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #7: Remedial action taken by the infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial action taken by the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking remedial steps — e.g., designing around, stopping infringing conduct, or other corrective steps — can mitigate against enhanced damages. Courts have refused enhancement where defendants took reasonable remedial or investigatory actions pre-suit (e.g., AVX, Blue Ridge X-Ray Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #8: The infringer's motivation for harm
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether the defendant acted with a motivation to harm the patentee; malicious or profit-motivated conduct weighs toward enhancement. The article lists motivation as one of the Read factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Factor #9: Whether the infringer attempted to conceal its misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the infringer attempted to conceal its misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to hide infringement or concealment efforts weigh in favor of enhanced damages. The article includes concealment as one of the nine Read factors considered by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Halo standard for enhanced damages (egregiousness; lowered burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Halo rejected Seagate's 'objective recklessness' requirement and lowered the burden of proof from 'clear and convincing' to a 'preponderance of the evidence,' focusing on 'egregiousness' centered on the subjective knowledge, intent, and behavior of the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court's Halo decision made it easier for patentees to obtain enhanced damages. The article explains that courts now assess willfulness through a holistic 'egregiousness' lens emphasizing subjective state of mind, and that the former post-hoc safe harbor (muster a reasonable defense at trial) under Seagate is gone. Cases like Dominion, Imperium, and SRI illustrate application of the post-Halo standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement: form reasonable non-infringement/invalidity positions during the infringement period
rubrics_metrics.description: Accused infringers must form reasonable non-infringement or invalidity positions during the actual period of infringement rather than relying on defenses first conjured after suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that Halo shifted the critical time to pre-litigation or contemporaneous with the infringing activity. Courts have held that creating an invalidity/non-infringement defense only after being sued is insufficient to avoid enhanced damages (see Dominion, Imperium, WBIP/Kohler discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a reasonable pre-suit investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable pre-suit investigation includes obtaining opinions of counsel, developing designs or processes to avoid infringement (design-arounds), and conducting competent technical and claim analyses by qualified individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples: AVX obtained pre-suit opinions of counsel and developed design-arounds and thus avoided enhancement; Blue Ridge's engineer-conducted pre-suit investigation supported absence of enhancement; Zoll's reasoned claim construction and reliance on the specification/prosecution history was 'reasonable.' By contrast, reliance on 'people without expertise in reading patent claims' or not reading patents until depositions (Cisco) was viewed negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary markers that courts consider (positive and negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts look to concrete evidence such as who reviewed patents and when, existence and quality of opinions of counsel, design-around efforts, testimony showing employees read (or failed to read) patents, and documented analyses/discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative markers: employees who didn't read patents until depositions (Cisco), beliefs based 'entirely on the opinion of people without expertise' (Dominion). Positive markers: documented counsel opinions obtained before litigation, documented design changes to avoid infringement, substantive technical analyses, and contemporaneous records of belief and investigation (AVX, Blue Ridge, Philips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical defense recommendation: implement early, documented patent-evaluation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants should have systems and processes to competently evaluate asserted patents early and collect documentation (analyses, documents, technical information, relevant discussions) to support a good faith belief of non-infringement or invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article's practical takeaway: implement procedures to evaluate patents contemporaneously with potential infringing activity; document investigations, opinions, and remedial efforts. Such proactive steps materially improve chances of avoiding enhanced damages under Halo.
